content.description: Delacroix painted the Three Glorious Days of July 1830: Marianne holding the flag, a mixed crowd, barricades. Political Romanticism walked into the museum.

hero.hook: One woman, one flag, and the Revolution becomes an image again.

blocks.text: In **1830**, [[The Three Glorious Days (July 27-29, 1830)]] drove King Charles X from the throne. **Eugène Delacroix** painted *Liberty Leading the People* at once.
Allegory and reportage blend together: this is [[Romanticism]] in action.
The Bourbon [[Restoration]] had disappointed. In three days, Paris filled with barricades. Delacroix himself was a bourgeois, yet he chose to celebrate the people in arms.
Delacroix put dead bodies in the foreground. Victory has a price. Liberty, one breast bare, is no distant goddess: she walks through the mud with the crowd.

blocks.caption: Liberty comes down into the street

blocks.text: The woman in the Phrygian cap embodies [[Marianne, symbol of the Republic]]. Around her: a worker, a bourgeois, a street boy close to Hugo's [[Gavroche]]. The painting unites the classes in revolt.
The tricolor flag structures the whole composition. Around it, the social classes mix for a moment. The image invents a visual brotherhood that real politics would fail to deliver.
Delacroix is said to have declared: “I have taken on a modern subject, a barricade.”
Shown at the [[Salons]], the painting quickly embarrassed [[Louis-Philippe I]], the new king. It was put away. Only later would it become a republican icon again.
Taken off the walls out of caution, the canvas waited for a more republican moment to become an icon again. The story of its reception is the story of 19th-century France.

blocks.caption: 1830: three days that changed the throne

blocks.text: Posters, banknotes, school memories: the image has outgrown the painting. It fixes the idea of a freedom won in the smoke.
To really grasp Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People, keep one thing in mind: every technical detail serves an emotion or an idea. The work is never merely decorative.
Context counts as much as style. Dates, places, patrons, audience: all of it explains why a form appears at one precise moment, and not before.
Finally, a legacy is measured over the long run. What we see today in museums, films, or popular music still carries the mark of these inventions.
From the street of 1830 to the school textbook, the painting set an image in place: freedom is won, not simply admired.
To really grasp Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People, keep one thing in mind: every technical detail serves an emotion or an idea. The work is never merely decorative.
Delacroix turned July 1830 into a living allegory: Marianne leads a mixed crowd over the barricades.

content.subject: art
content.title: What does Delacroix's “Liberty Leading the People” celebrate?

Gavroche.explanation: The child hero of Victor Hugo's 'Les Misérables', inspired by the boy with pistols in Delacroix's painting.

July 27-29, 1830.explanation: Three revolutionary days that overthrew King Charles X, who wanted to suppress freedom of the press and reduce voting rights. Louis Philippe I took the constitutional throne in his place.

July Revolution (July 27-29, 1830).explanation: Three revolutionary days that overthrew King Charles X, who wanted to suppress freedom of the press and reduce voting rights. Louis Philippe I took the constitutional throne in his place.

Louis-Philippe I.explanation: The last King of the French (1830-1848), who came to power after the July Revolution; he purchased the painting by Delacroix before hiding it because he judged it too subversive.

Marianne, symbol of the Republic.explanation: An allegorical female figure embodying the French Republic since the Revolution. Her Phrygian cap (a symbol of ancient freedom) is her distinctive attribute. Delacroix's Liberty is its founding image, reproduced in every town hall in France.

Restoration.explanation: A period in French history (1814-1830) marked by the return of the Bourbon kings, Louis XVIII and then Charles X, after the fall of Napoleon.

Romanticism.explanation: 19th-century art movement favoring the expression of feelings, imagination, and dynamism over classical rigor. Delacroix is its main representative in painting.

Salons.explanation: Official exhibitions organized by the Academy of Fine Arts in Paris, where artists presented their works to the public and critics.

The Three Glorious Days.explanation: Three revolutionary days that overthrew King Charles X, who wanted to suppress freedom of the press and reduce voting rights. Louis Philippe I took the constitutional throne in his place.
